abstract: Research in auditory and visual fields has shown that false percepts can emerge when perceptual priors outweigh incoming sensory information. However, the role of similar top-down mechanisms in generating false percepts in the olfactory domain is less understood. To address this, we implemented a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm in which we first individually determined the odor detection thresholds of Butanol (n = 55) using an adaptive algorithm. Participants then completed an odor detection task where on each trial one of two distinct visual cues was paired with either a supra-threshold, threshold, or sub-threshold concentration of Butanol, or no odor. In the first three trial blocks, one visual stimulus (strong cue) was paired more frequently with supra-threshold concentrations, and the other visual stimulus (weak cue) was paired more frequently with sub-threshold concentrations. In the last three blocks both cues were paired most frequently with the no odor condition. We observed significantly greater odor detection rates on no odor trials for the strong cue compared to the weak cue. Importantly, this finding could not be explained by differences in total number of visual cue presentations or other task variables. Further, the difference in odor detection rate for the strong and weak cues during the supra-threshold conditioning trials predicted the difference in false odor detection during the no odor trials, suggesting that the prior formed between the strong cue and odor contributed to the false olfactory percepts. This demonstrates that false odor perception can be enhanced by the expectation of an olfactory stimulus in a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm. These findings could yield therapeutic insight into the mechanisms underlying pathological olfactory hallucinations.
